blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a critical case study on the need for adversarial thinking in IoT and smart city deployments, particularly given the rapid rollout of connected vehicle technology by the USDOT. The paper demonstrates how a single malicious vehicle can exploit weaknesses in the I-SIG (Intelligent Traffic Signal) system, which uses connected vehicle data to optimize traffic light timing. The authors show that data spoofing attacks can reverse the system's benefits: increasing total traffic delay by up to 68.1% and even causing complete gridlock at junctions. The key insight is that the COP algorithm's reliance on limited look-ahead stages (only two) and its sensitivity to the 'last vehicle' in a queue makes it highly vulnerable to manipulation, even without compromising cryptographic protections like PKI-signed BSM messages. The paper underscores the risks of deploying systems without rigorous adversarial testing.
paper_title: Exposing Congestion Attack on Emerging Connected Vehicle Based Signal Traffic Control
paper_abstract: —We address the security of a network of Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) cooperating to safely navigate through a conflict area (e.g., traffic intersections, merging roadways, roundabouts). Previous studies have shown that such a network can be targeted by adversarial attacks causing traffic jams or safety violations ending in collisions. We focus on attacks targeting the V2X communication network used to share vehicle data and consider as well uncertainties due to noise in sensor measurements and communication channels. To combat these, motivated by recent work on the safe control of CAVs, we propose a trust-aware robust event-triggered decentralized control and coordination framework that can provably guarantee safety. We maintain a trust metric for each vehicle in the network computed based on their behavior and used to balance the tradeoff between conservativeness (when deeming every vehicle as untrustworthy) and guaranteed safety and security. It is important to highlight that our framework is invariant to the specific choice of the trust framework. Based on this framework, we propose an attack detection and mitigation scheme which has twofold benefits: (i) the trust framework is immune to false positives, and (ii) it provably guarantees safety against false positive cases. We use extensive simulations (in SUMO and CARLA) to validate the theoretical guarantees and demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed scheme to detect and mitigate adversarial attacks. The code for the simulated scenarios can be found in this link. I. I NTRODUCTION The emergence of Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) and advancements in traffic infrastructure [1] promise to offer solutions to transportation issues like accidents, congestion, energy consumption, and pollution [2], [3].
